newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crew takes break as Mir steadied on course.
newsitem.headline: Crew takes break as Mir steadied on course.

text.p: The accident-prone crew of Russia's Mir space station finally arrested their tumble through space on Friday, locking the crippled ship's solar panels on to the Sun and switching the lights back on.
"We solved the problem," NASA official Mark Severance told Reuters at Mission Control outside Moscow, praising a long night's work by Russian flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin.
"Things are going real well. I'm really pleased."
The calamity has, however, probably put paid to plans for Lazutkin and NASA physicist Michael Foale to make risky repairs to power cables severed after a near-fatal collision on June 25.
Deputy mission director Sergei Krikalyov told reporters it was "very likely" that the difficult rewiring job would now be put off for a relief crew due to arrive at Mir on August 7.

Lazutkin toiled through the night to reconnect most of its life-support systems some 24 hours after one of the three crew -- officials will not say who -- mistakenly pulled out a cable and crashed the on-board computer, plunging Mir into darkness.
"We established orientation about 4 a.m. (midnight GMT)," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told a news conference.
"All microclimate systems are working completely normally. The conditions are completely comfortable."

Lazutkin, 39, worked on after his two crewmates went to bed. But he will join Russian commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who has developed a stress-induced heart problem, and the British-born Foale, 40, in taking most of Friday off.
"We have decided to allow them to rest," Solovyov said, giving the three men the chance to kick back and watch videos, read or listen to music after the stress of the previous day.
They might even get a chance to talk to their wives.

Thursday's pulled plug threw the sprawling and already underpowered 140-tonne complex into a spin, depriving its solar panels of a steady stream of rays. It forced the crew to switch off systems and rely on back-up from their Soyuz escape capsule.
After slowly recharging its batteries, the station, which has suffered a jinx-like sequence of mishaps this year, is now being held in alignment by electronically controlled motors.
The gyroscope system that orients Mir without using up fuel, is to be reconnected late on Friday. Other remaining systems can then be hooked up again.
By the end of the day Mir should then be back to the condition it was in on Wednesday, when the experienced Tsibliyev, 43, was taken off the repair team and Foale asked to back up Lazutkin.
Lazutkin, on his first space mission, literally had a baptism of fire when a blaze broke out on Mir in February.

The moustachioed rocket scientist and former gymnast, who has had much less media attention than his two comrades, was due to perform the most dangerous task -- opening up the Spektr science module. It was sealed off three weeks ago after an unmanned craft manoeuvred by Tsibliyev smashed a hole in it.
The cosmonauts do not know what conditions are like in Spektr, what poisonous substances or sharp objects may be lurking in its cramped airless interior.
Lazutkin, in a clumsy spacesuit with Foale as back-up, was due to go into Spektr around July 24 to reconnect cables to solar panels whose loss has cut Mir's power supply by up to half.
But officials, faced with a wait of at least a week in any case while the stand-in Foale receives last-minute special training, now seem likely to put the task off.
A relief crew has been practising on Earth for both the rewiring and for a spacewalk to try to seal the puncture.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Mission Control official saying Frenchman Leopold Eyharts could be dropped from the next flight, letting his two Russian colleagues fly in more supplies. "Changes in the flight plan are always possible," Solovyov said.

The problems have raised questions over whether Mir should be ditched before a new international space station is launched next year. If the crew abandoned ship, the station would die within days and eventually come crashing back to Earth.
But Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they do not want to abandon the station.
